note:
The people of Israel, back in their land after the exile, are not convinced that God loves them. This section is God’s response to that cynical doubt. The Lord reminds Israel that Jacob, her ancestor, was chosen by God while Esau, Edom’s forefather, was rejected. Therefore, although Israel has experienced the Lord’s wrath for just a little while, Edom is a “people with whom the LORD is angry forever” (1:4). Furthermore, while Israel is heir of the everlasting promises of their covenant Lord, Edom will never rise again. The Lord’s judgment on Edom will be cause for praise in Israel.

**1:1 oracle of the word.** Is. 13:1; Nah. 1:1; Hab. 1:1; Zech. 9:1; 12:1. Normally used in prophecies of judgment, “oracle” may point to the urgency felt by the prophet in issuing his proclamation. On this urgency, see also Jer. 20:9; Amos 3:8.

**Malachi.** This could be either a personal name or a title (Introduction: Title and Author).

God’s electing love is sovereign and unconditional. It is expounded principally in Deuteronomy, where the verbs “to choose” and “to love” are parallel, showing that love is not a feeling but the behavior that flows from a committed relationship (Deut. 7:6–8). God’s love is manifested in the covenant He initiates with His people. The nearness of God to Israel was to be the source of awe and amazement (Deut. 4:7, 8). God’s love begins in eternity (Jer. 31:3) and is manifested in His covenantal dealings with Abraham, Israel, and David (Gen. 17; Ex. 19:5, 6; 2 Sam. 7). God’s election of Jacob continues to have relevance for His dealings with Israel in the period of Malachi’s ministry. Properly understood, God’s love does not lead to moral complacency but to moral zeal. However, Israel’s complacency and the people’s cynicism about God’s love have led to the moral crises that Malachi addresses. See theological note “Predestination.”

**How have you loved us.** The response of Malachi’s hearers might be surprising given all that the Lord has done for His people throughout the OT. Yet at this point in their history, perhaps a century after the return from the exile, it reflects the difficult challenges of life in a vassal state of Persia. The people are asking, “Where are all of the great blessings God has promised through His prophets?”

**Jacob.** One of the titles for God in the Psalms is “the God of Jacob” (Pss. 20:1; 46:7; 75:9; 76:6; 84:8). God’s electing love is unique because He loves sinners, who by nature are the objects of His displeasure and wrath (Luke 15:2; Rom. 5:6–8; Eph. 2:1–3). The history of Jacob and Esau in Genesis clearly points to God’s choice of Jacob despite his lack of merit (Gen. 25:21–34; 27:1–40; Rom. 9:10–13).

Although there is a usage of the verb “hate” which means “to love less” (Gen. 29:31; Luke 14:26), the context immediately following suggests that here “hate” means active rejection, displeasure, and disfavor manifested in retributive justice. Like love (1:2 note), hatred is not merely an emotion but a covenantal term that includes the actions that flow from it. It is not merely that Esau (and the nation that comes from him, Edom) suffers the absence or lessening of blessing, but that he receives judgment that works its way out in the course of history. For this usage of “hate,” see Ps. 5:5; Is. 61:8; Hos. 9:15; Amos 5:21; Mal. 2:16. See theological note “Predestination and Reprobation” on p. 1997. Neither Jacob (Israel) nor Esau (Edom) deserves God’s love. Both merit destruction. Yet because of God’s electing love for Jacob, Israel will be restored after her deserved punishment at the hands of the Babylonians, while Edom will have no such restoration. This distinction should encourage the Jews of Malachi’s day to recognize the Lord’s utterly undeserved mercy to them.

**laid waste.** Probably a reference to the occupation of Edom by the Nabatean Arabs.

God is the sovereign Lord of history, whose redemptive purposes are accomplished both inside and outside ancient Israel (v. 11; Gen. 17:4–6). The fact that there is still a territory that could be called “Israel” in Malachi’s day is a mark of God’s faithfulness to His promises. In contrast, the land of Edom will disappear forever.

A major reason for the Lord’s anger with Israel is the priesthood’s attitude toward God’s name at the altar and toward God’s law in teaching and judging. At the altar, they offer diseased or imperfect animals in sacrifice, thereby reversing the intent of their labors and bringing curse and defilement where they should bring blessing and cleansing. In their teaching and judging, they violate the covenant with Levi (2:8), showing partiality and causing many to stumble.

**1:6 honor.** If normal fathers and masters expected honor, how much more does God deserve honor? God is in Himself infinitely glorious, and He must receive the recognition of His people (Pss. 29:1, 2; 57:5, 11).

**despise.** The opposite of honoring and fearing the Lord (cf. 2 Sam. 12:9, 10). The word is used often in Proverbs (1:7; 15:20; 23:22).

The reference is to animal sacrifices (v. 8). “Polluted” means ceremonially unclean and therefore unacceptable to God. God is not offended merely by ceremonial imperfections but by the attitude of contempt behind such imperfect sacrifices (Gen. 4:3–5 and notes; Heb. 11:4). The priests’ task is to teach the law and to oversee the sacrifices, so they are culpable for allowing the people to bring such defective offerings.

**the LORD’s table.** This phrase and the similar phrase in v. 12 occur only here in the OT, both times referring to the altar.

The law expressly prohibits such offerings (Lev. 22:22; Deut. 15:21). Only unblemished animals are suitable, prefiguring the perfect atonement that Christ would ultimately make for sin.

**to your governor.** It is normal in Malachi’s culture for a visitor to bring a gift to a superior; someone who brings a defective animal as a gift, however, should hardly expect to receive a favorable welcome.

Even worship that is offered in the right location in the name of the true God is not acceptable if it comes from a defiled heart. The Lord prefers that no offerings be presented on His altar rather than such defective ones.

verse_quote: my name will be great among the nations.
note:
In contrast to the despising of His name by the priests (v. 6), God promises the future triumph of His glorious kingdom. “From the rising of the sun to its setting” and similar phrases often point to God’s future judgment of the entire world and the restoration of His order (Ps. 50:1; Is. 45:6; 59:19).

**in every place.** The imperfect sacrifices being offered during the prophet’s time (vv. 7, 8) are contrasted with the pure offerings of worship in the future (Is. 2:2–4; 66:19–21; Zech. 14:16–21). The promise of this verse is being fulfilled even now as Christ gathers His royal priests from among the nations (1 Pet. 2:9; Rev. 5:9, 10), and it will be consummated in the future as the nations gather to worship God in purity (Rev. 21:27).
In the similar phrase in v. 7, “the LORD” is the divine name, Yahweh. Here it is “Lord,” the same word for “master” in v. 6, underlining the lack of respect that is being shown to God.

Laws regulating offerings given in response to a vow require the giving of a perfect offering. This text implies an attempt to deceive the Lord by promising a costly offering when in trouble but then giving a less-expensive offering after deliverance has been granted (cf. Ps. 76:11).

**I am a great King.** God is not only their Father (1:6; Ex. 4:22) and their Master but also their King. The idea of God as King arose early in OT religion (Ex. 15:18; Num. 23:21; 24:7; Deut. 33:5). See Pss. 93–100.
The priests are supposed to be the representatives of the people as well as their spiritual leaders. The following verses show how they have failed to act in accordance with their priestly calling.

verse_quote: I will send the curse upon you.
note:
See Deut. 28:20.

**I will curse your blessings.** The blessings are either the physical and material blessings promised to the priests who receive the people’s tithes (Num. 18:21) or the pronouncements of blessing uttered by the priests at the time of the sacrifices (Num. 6:24–27), which then become a curse.

Lit. “I will rebuke your seed” (text note). This could mean a curse on the priest’s offspring or a literal curse on their agricultural seed (cf. Lev. 26:16; Deut. 28:38). Or, both could be in view.

**spread dung on your faces.** Refers to the animal intestines and their excretory contents, which are a byproduct of the sacrificial process.
This covenant includes Levi’s descendants, entitling them to a hereditary priesthood (cf. Ex. 32:29; Num. 25:11–13; Jer. 33:20, 21).

The central thrust of Deuteronomy is to show the connection between covenant obedience and life. Commitment to God leads to a full life. Some see in “covenant ... of ... peace” an allusion to the covenant with Phinehas mentioned in Num. 25:10–13.

verse_quote: lips of a priest should guard knowledge.
note:
See Ezra 7:10; Hos. 4:6. The connection between the true knowledge of the Lord and priestly instruction in the law is set forth vividly in 2 Chr. 15:3: “For a long time Israel was without the true God, and without a teaching priest and without law.” Providing this instruction is the first task of the priesthood (Deut. 33:10).

**messenger of the LORD of hosts.** The Hb. word translated “messenger” is the same one elsewhere translated “angel,” underlining the authority with which the priests speak.

verse_quote: you have turned aside from the way.
note: See Neh. 13:29. The priests’ attitudes and actions set a bad example for the people. They have abandoned their true calling, both to teach and practice the truth. Instead of turning people from iniquity (v. 7), they actually are actually leading the people off the true path.

The basis for this censure is the character of God. God “is not partial and takes no bribe” (Deut. 10:17; cf. Lev. 19:15). Possibly the priests are favoring society’s rich and powerful people at the expense of the poor and powerless.

Lack of faithfulness toward God leads to breakdowns in human relationships. Malachi addresses two problems: marriage to idolatrous wives (vv. 10–12) and the divorcing of Israelite wives (vv. 13–16).

**2:10 one Father.** Some interpret this as referring to Abraham (Is. 51:2). More likely it refers to God (1:6; Ex. 4:22, 23; Deut. 32:6; Is. 63:16; 64:8; Jer. 3:4, 19; 31:9). As a good Father, He will discipline the disobedient (Heb. 12:5–11).

This verb is used five times in vv. 10–16. In Jer. 3:20, it refers to marital unfaithfulness; more generally, it applies to any breach of covenant obligations.

**abomination.** The Hb. word here, prominently employed in Deuteronomy, refers to idolatrous religious practices (Deut. 7:25, 26; 12:31; 13:14; 18:12). It can also refer to sexual transgression (Lev. 18:22, 26, 29, 30; Deut. 24:4).

**profaned the sanctuary of the LORD.** The Hb. word translated “sanctuary” can also be understood as referring to the people themselves (“holy seed”; Is. 6:13; cf. Ezra 9:2). The people, who are loved by God, defile themselves by disobedience in their marriage practices.

**married the daughter of a foreign god.** This phrase refers to marrying a woman still committed to a foreign god—an idolater outside the covenant (cf. Gen. 24:3, 4; Ex. 34:12–16; Deut. 7:3, 4; Josh. 23:12; 1 Kin. 11:1–10). The prohibition against marrying unbelievers continues in the NT (1 Cor. 7:39; 2 Cor. 6:14).

verse_quote: cover the LORD’s altar with tears.
note: These are not the marks of true repentance here; the people’s actions demonstrate them to be an empty gesture, more in line with pagan rituals than with the true worship of God.

See v. 15; Prov. 5:18. The motivation for abandoning these marriages may be romantic or to pursue politically advantageous relationships with the surrounding ethnic groups, who hold a great deal of power.

**your companion.** A related form of this unique word is used to describe a seam or a joint in a building, or the process of cementing something together.

**your wife by covenant.** God’s covenant faithfulness is to be mirrored in the marriage relationships of His people (Prov. 2:17; Eph. 5:22–33).

See Gen. 2:24.

**portion of the Spirit.** The marriage union is not merely physical but spiritual as well, and has as its goal godly offspring for God Himself.

See Is. 50:1; Deut. 24:1–4; theological note “Marriage” above, and “Divorce” on p. 1755. As in 1:3, “hate” is a covenantal word that describes the rejection of relationship.

**garment.** Entering into marriage and obtaining a wife is sometimes portrayed as covering with a garment (Ruth 3:9 text note; Ezek. 16:8). Abusing and divorcing a wife metaphorically stains a person’s garment, making him unfit to enter God’s presence.

Religious cynics charge the Lord with injustice. God responds with the promise that He will send a messenger to prepare the way before Him before returning to His temple. His presence among a wicked people requires judgment and gracious refinement (3:2, 3). He will change the Levites’ hearts and they will offer sacrifices in righteousness once again. The judgment will be exacting (3:5). The Lord Himself will be the chief witness for the prosecution of His people.

**2:17 wearied the LORD.** See Is. 43:24. In Malachi, the offenses revolve around the cynical rejection of God’s moral government and the attendant insolent spirit that constantly puts God on trial.

**Everyone who does evil is good.** This is an explicit rejection of the Lord’s statement in Deut. 18:12. They stumble over the same issues that caused the psalmist difficulties in Ps. 73.

This section rebuts two cynical statements from ch. 2. First, the allegation in 2:17 that God does not differentiate between good and evil is answered in 3:2 by referring to the refining and purifying ministry of the messenger of the covenant. The second statement, “Where is the God of justice?” (2:17), is answered in v. 5. The Jews in Malachi’s day are looking for the Lord to judge the nations, but instead the Lord will come near to _them_ for judgment (v. 5).

**3:1 my messenger.** See 4:5; also Is. 40:3 (where “prepare the way” also occurs). It was the practice in the ancient Near East to send messengers in advance of a visiting king to announce his coming and to remove all hindrances or obstacles. This prophetic messenger (Matt. 11:10) will be the last of his kind to appear before the coming of the Lord, who is “the messenger of the covenant.”

**suddenly.** This word is almost always associated in Scripture with an unhappy and calamitous circumstance (Num. 12:4; Is. 47:11; cf. 2 Pet. 3:10).

**the messenger of the covenant.** A person distinct from “my messenger,” He will purify the sacrifices, the priests, and the nation (vv. 2–5). This “messenger of the covenant” is the Messiah, and this prophecy is fulfilled in Jesus, who alone has performed the perfect sacrifice on behalf of His people.
Ancient launderers used harsh chemicals extracted from plants to remove stubborn stains from clothing

verse_quote: he will purify the sons of Levi.
note:
The priests have been instrumental in leading the people astray. The work of purification will begin with them, and it will spread from them to the whole of the nation. The Levites are the pattern for the nation, which is to be “a kingdom of priests” (Ex. 19:6). Silver is harder to purify than gold.

**offerings in righteousness.** See “a pure offering” in 1:11. Because of the work of the messenger of the covenant, proper worship will again be offered, since the hearts and lives of the worshipers will be purified (Ps. 4:5; Zeph. 3:9).

verse_quote: Then I will draw near to you for judgment.
note: This section began with the religious cynics’ accusing the Lord of injustice. It ends with a covenant lawsuit in which the Lord brings charges against His people. The seven specific sins mentioned in v. 5 are a broad cross section of offenses clearly forbidden in the law of God. The root cause of these sins is that they “do not fear me.”

The people are not only bringing defective offerings but also are withholding the tithe, apparently due to the crops’ meager returns. But withholding the tithe is stealing from the Lord. As a consequence, the righteous Lord withholds blessing. Their sin also evidences a lack of trust in the Lord to provide for their needs if they keep His commands. So, the Lord urges them to put Him to the test. If they do so, the consequent provision will be so great that the nations will see the difference and pronounce Israel blessed.

**3:6 I ... do not change.** The immutability, or unchangeable character, of God is seen in His purpose to bless His elect people. Thus, in spite of their numerous sins, they are not destroyed (Ex. 34:6, 7; Jer. 30:11). This verse closes the previous section and begins the next one.

verse_quote: Return to me, and I will return to you.
note:
The command to repent is connected with a promise (cf. Zech. 1:3; James 4:8). Sin separates people from God and causes God to hide His face (Is. 59:2).

**How shall we return.** This is not a genuine question; there is plenty of information on how to return to the Lord in the Scriptures that they already possessed.

Lit. “a tenth.” The practice of tithing is mentioned in the accounts of Abraham (Gen. 14:20) and Jacob (Gen. 28:22), and is codified in the law of Moses as an annual requirement to bring in one-tenth of the agricultural produce as a mark of the Lord’s ownership of the Promised Land (Lev. 27:30; Num. 18:26; Deut. 14:22–29).

**contributions.** Portions of the animal sacrifices to which the priests are entitled (Ex. 29:27, 28; Lev. 9:22).

Refers to a room in the temple designated for the storage of gifts so that they can be distributed to the priests and the Levites, as well as to the poor of the community (2 Chr. 31:11; Neh. 10:38, 39; 12:44; 13:12).

**put me to the test.** This is a reversal of the ordinary biblical pattern, in which God typically tests human beings (Pss. 11:5; 26:2; 66:10; Prov. 17:3; Jer. 11:20; 12:3; 17:10). Only in a few instances are humans invited to test God (i.e., to prove His claims and justify His commands; Is. 7:11, 12; 1 Kin. 18:22–46). Because the tithe is a covenantal obligation under the Sinai covenant, specific blessings and curses were attached to it. Under the new covenant, Paul calls us to excel in the grace of giving (2 Cor. 8:7). This suggests that love should move us to greater generosity than the law ever could, and that the old covenant tithe is really just the minimum that people should give to God’s work.

**windows of heaven.** See Gen. 7:11. Rain in its appropriate time is a blessing from the Lord and is crucial to the agricultural well-being of the community.

In addition to providing the all-important rain, the Lord also promises to protect the crops against destructive pests, which are themselves a sign of covenant curse under the Mosaic covenant (see Deut. 28:38–42). The result of these blessings will be fruitful harvests.

The last section returns to the prophecy in 3:1–5 concerning the forerunner (Matt. 11:10) and the coming of God. In various ways, the beginning of the section is reminiscent of a psalm of lament. The complaints, however, are interpreted as hard words against the Lord. Yet there are those who sense the same injustices without concluding that it is futile to serve the Lord. The first group speaks hard words and invites the Lord’s response; the latter fears the Lord and so He writes words of remembrance concerning them. He promises that they will be His special possession in the great day of the Lord.

A reference to “the day” (v. 17) again introduces the last day of judgment, a day of destruction for the wicked but healing for the righteous. The final verses return to the promised forerunner and exhort the people to keep the law of Moses.

**3:13Your words have been hard.** This aptly describes the people’s responses to the Lord throughout the book of Malachi, which have revealed the corresponding hardness of their hearts. Instead of repenting, the people consistently have contested the validity of each of the Lord’s charges against them.

Lit. “empty” or “useless.” The hardness of the people’s hearts is revealed by their response to the prosperity of the wicked. They have concluded that serving the Lord is worthless.

**profit.** The Hb. term usually refers to unjust gain. Greed is inconsistent with a desire for God’s truth (Ps. 119:36).

Typically an expression of blatant unbelief (Num. 14:22; Deut. 6:16; Ps. 95:9; Matt. 4:7). Rarely, the Lord actually invites people to put Him to the test, in which case to decline is a sign of unbelief (3:10 note).

The conversation and conduct of those who fear God is occasioned by the preceding words of murmuring and is placed in contrast to them. Instead of speaking hard words against God, this group esteems the Lord’s name.

**book of remembrance.** This exact phrase is found only here, but references to a special book are found elsewhere (Ex. 32:32; Ps. 69:28; Dan. 7:10). This provides the answer to those who earlier asked, “Where is the God of justice?” (2:17). The Lord is aware of what is happening and watching over those who truly belong to Him.

Refers to the remnant described in v. 16.

**my treasured possession.** In the early stage of OT revelation, the nation of Israel is called God’s “treasured possession” (Ex. 19:5; Deut. 7:6; 14:2). On the day when the Lord constitutes this precious remnant, it will become clear to all that serving the Lord has not, in fact, been in vain (3:14).

**his son who serves him.** See 1:6.

Two images of fire are used in Malachi to describe the Lord: a refining fire (3:2) and a destroying fire (4:1). Evildoers do not actually put the Lord to the test and escape (see 3:15).

**root nor branch.** The wicked are compared to a tree (Amos 2:9) that will be totally destroyed, consumed from the topmost branch down to the roots.

An expression unique to Malachi (cf. Ps. 84:12). The Davidic king will reign in righteousness (Is. 32:1) and will be called “a righteous Branch” (Jer. 23:5, 6). The rising sun reveals the truth about the Lord and His people, vindicating those who are faithful and condemning those who remain rebellious.

**healing in its wings.** The Bible considers physical sickness and spiritual sickness or sin to be analogous. Salvation is often compared to bodily healing (Ex. 15:26; 2 Chr. 7:14; Ps. 103:3; Is. 53:5; Jer. 17:14). The sun was often depicted in antiquity as a winged disk.

**calves from the stall.** Calves that have been specially fattened and are full of vigor.
Patience is required until the day when God acts to demonstrate the decisive difference between the fate of the righteous and the wicked.

verse_quote: Remember the law of my servant Moses.
note: Together, Moses and Elijah (v. 5) represent the Law and the Prophets. Moses communicated God’s law with its statutes and rules, which the priests have been failing to teach the people (2:6). However, the righteous remnant will remember them.

verse_quote: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet.
note: The task of the prophets is to convict those who have failed to heed the law of Moses and to call them to repentance for their sin. The literary connection of this verse with 3:1 indicates that “Elijah” is the same person as “my messenger.” Both verses begin with the word “Behold” and use the same form of the verb “to send.” In both cases, the mission is to bring repentance in advance of the coming day of the Lord. The NT identifies this “Elijah” as John the Baptist, who epitomized the prophet’s message of judgment and repentance (Matt. 11:14; 17:10; Mark 9:11–13; Luke 1:17).

verse_quote: turn the hearts of fathers to their children.
note:
Repentance and turning to God will be seen in the restoration of family relationships (Luke 1:17). Since God is our Father (1:6), repentance also means restoration in that relationship as well.

**lest I come and strike the land with a decree.** Malachi began with the announcement of God’s electing love, yet the book ends with the threat of a curse. Malachi’s dual thrust of mercy and judgment is echoed by Paul’s pronouncement, “Note then the kindness and the severity of God” (Rom. 11:22; cf. Deut. 30:19, 20). Strikingly, Luke 1:17 focuses on the positive side of Malachi’s prophecy, for in His first coming Jesus came to seek and to save that which was lost. Yet those who refuse the salvation that Christ came to bring will face another coming in which Jesus rides out to bring destruction on the unrepentant (Rev. 19:11–21).
